topics.title: Basis of classification: levels of organisation, gut and circulation

learn.hook: A sponge and a cheetah are both animals, yet one is a loose bag of cells and the other a high-speed machine. How do we compare them fairly?
points: Animals differ hugely in structure, but share fundamental features (arrangement of cells, body symmetry, coelom, digestive, circulatory and reproductive patterns) that are used for classification.

Levels of organisation: cellular level in sponges (loose cell aggregates); tissue level in coelenterates; organ level in Platyhelminthes; organ-system level in annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates.
Incomplete digestive system: a single opening serves as both mouth and anus (e.g. Platyhelminthes). Complete digestive system: two openings, mouth and anus.

Open circulatory system: blood is pumped out of the heart and cells and tissues are directly bathed in it (e.g. arthropods, molluscs). Closed circulatory system: blood flows through a series of vessels of varying diameters (e.g. annelids, chordates).

example.q: A flatworm takes food in and throws undigested waste out through the same opening. What type of digestive system is this?
steps: Only one opening to the gut.
One opening working as both mouth and anus means an incomplete digestive system.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways uses a 'closed' system of pipes for train brakes; a garden sprinkler is 'open'. Animal circulation follows the same two designs.

quiz.q: Sponges show which level of organisation?
quiz.explain: Sponge cells are loose aggregates without true tissues.
steps: Sponges are loose aggregates of cells without true tissues.
That is the cellular level of organisation.
Tissue level begins with coelenterates.
Answer: Cellular level

quiz.q: In an open circulatory system:
quiz.explain: Open systems lack a continuous network of vessels; tissues are bathed in blood.
steps: In open circulation, the heart pumps blood out of vessels.
Cells and tissues are directly bathed in blood.
Blood staying in vessels describes closed circulation.
Answer: Blood is pumped out of the heart and bathes cells and tissues directly
options: Blood is pumped out of the heart and bathes cells and tissues directly

quiz.q: A complete digestive system has:
quiz.explain: Complete means separate entry (mouth) and exit (anus).
steps: Complete digestive system = separate entry and exit.
It has two openings: mouth and anus.
One opening means incomplete.
Answer: Two openings, a mouth and an anus
options: Two openings, a mouth and an anus

quiz.q: Coelenterates show which level of organisation?
quiz.explain: Cells in coelenterates are arranged into tissues.
steps: Coelenterate cells are arranged into tissues.
So they show tissue level.
Sponges are cellular; Platyhelminthes are organ level.
Answer: Tissue level

quiz.q: Which animal has a closed circulatory system?
quiz.explain: Annelids such as the earthworm have closed circulation; arthropods and molluscs like Pila have open circulation.
steps: Closed circulation: blood flows in vessels (annelids, chordates).
Prawn and cockroach are arthropods, Pila a mollusc: open circulation.
Earthworm is an annelid, so it has closed circulation.
Answer: Earthworm
quiz.mistake: Thinks all invertebrates have open circulation

quiz.q: Members of Platyhelminthes show which level of organisation?
quiz.explain: Platyhelminthes are the first with tissues grouped into organs.
steps: In Platyhelminthes, tissues are grouped into organs.
That is the organ level.
Organ-system level starts with annelids and arthropods.
Answer: Organ level

quiz.q: Why are fundamental features used to classify animals?
quiz.explain: Shared fundamental features reveal relationships despite structural differences.
steps: Animals differ greatly in form.
Basic features (cell arrangement, symmetry, coelom, gut, circulation) are shared by related animals.
So these fundamental features reveal relationships.
Answer: Animals differ in form, but common basic features like symmetry and coelom show relationships
options: Every animal is unique, so no grouping is possible
Animals differ in form, but common basic features like symmetry and coelom show relationships

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Flatworms have an incomplete digestive system. Reason (R): In flatworms the gut has only one opening to the outside.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; a single opening is what makes the system incomplete.
steps: A: flatworms have an incomplete digestive system. True.
R: their gut has only one opening. True.
A single opening is what makes it incomplete, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R defines A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can a sponge and a tiger both be animals?' Explain the bases used to group animals!
teach.praise: Tweet! Levels of organisation, gut type and circulation. Now I can compare anything!
teach.nudge: Good! What levels of organisation are there, and what is open vs closed circulation?

revise.summary: Animals are classified using fundamental features. Levels of organisation run from cellular (sponges) to tissue (coelenterates), organ (flatworms) and organ-system (annelids onwards). Guts are incomplete or complete; circulation is open or closed.

Incomplete vs complete digestive system
Open vs closed circulatory system with examples
remember: Cellular: Porifera; tissue: Coelenterata; organ: Platyhelminthes; organ-system: annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms, chordates
Incomplete gut: one opening; complete: mouth and anus
Open: arthropods, molluscs; closed: annelids, chordates
traps: Don't give molluscs or arthropods closed circulation
Don't put flatworms at organ-system level; they are at organ level

learn.hook: Cut a starfish like a pizza and every slice looks alike. Cut yourself (only in imagination!) and only one cut gives two mirror halves.
points: Asymmetrical: no plane divides the body into equal halves (most sponges).
Radial symmetry: any plane through the central axis gives two identical halves (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms).
Bilateral symmetry: only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves (annelids, arthropods and others).
Diploblastic animals have two germ layers, external ectoderm and internal endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea in between (coelenterates).
Triploblastic animals have a third germ layer, mesoderm, between ectoderm and endoderm (Platyhelminthes to chordates).

example.q: A Hydra has ectoderm and endoderm with a jelly-like layer in between. Classify its germ-layer organisation and symmetry.
steps: Two germ layers with mesoglea between them: diploblastic.
Coelenterates are radially symmetrical.

learn.reallife: Starfish found in tide pools along the Gujarat and Goa coasts are bilaterally symmetrical as larvae but become radially symmetrical as adults.

games.title: Germ layers
items: They have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea.
Mesoglea is a true germ layer.
It is an undifferentiated layer, not mesoderm.
Larvae are bilateral; adults are radial.
Only one plane gives mirror halves.
Mesoderm lies between ectoderm and endoderm.
It is the middle germ layer.

quiz.q: Animals in which any plane through the central axis gives identical halves show:
quiz.explain: Radial symmetry: many planes through the axis divide the body equally.
steps: If any plane through the central axis gives identical halves, there are many planes of symmetry.
That is radial symmetry.
Bilateral has only one such plane.
Answer: Radial symmetry

quiz.q: Which group is diploblastic?
quiz.explain: Coelenterates (and ctenophores) have only two germ layers.
steps: Diploblastic = two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm.
Coelenterates (and ctenophores) are diploblastic.
Arthropods, chordates and annelids are triploblastic.
Answer: Coelenterates

quiz.q: The undifferentiated layer between ectoderm and endoderm in diploblastic animals is the:
quiz.explain: Mesoglea is jelly-like and not a germ layer.
steps: Diploblastic animals have a jelly-like layer between ectoderm and endoderm.
It is the undifferentiated mesoglea, not a germ layer.
Mesoderm is a true germ layer found in triploblastic animals.
Answer: Mesoglea

quiz.q: Most sponges are:
quiz.explain: No plane divides most sponges into equal halves.
steps: No plane divides most sponges into equal halves.
So most sponges are asymmetrical.
Answer: Asymmetrical

quiz.q: Which group shows radial symmetry in adults but bilateral symmetry in larvae?
quiz.explain: Echinoderm larvae are bilateral; adults become radial.
steps: Echinoderm larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
Adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical.
Answer: Echinodermata
quiz.mistake: Does not know the echinoderm larva

quiz.q: Triploblastic organisation first appears in:
quiz.explain: Platyhelminthes onwards have mesoderm.
steps: Triploblastic = has mesoderm as a third germ layer.
Mesoderm first appears in Platyhelminthes.
Porifera, Coelenterata and Ctenophora lack it.
Answer: Platyhelminthes

quiz.q: Bilateral symmetry means:
quiz.explain: Bilateral animals have a single plane of symmetry.
steps: Bilateral symmetry has a single plane of symmetry.
It divides the body into identical left and right halves.
Many planes would be radial symmetry.
Answer: Only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves
options: Any plane through the axis gives identical halves
Only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ctenophores are diploblastic. Reason (R): Ctenophores have ectoderm, endoderm and a well-formed mesoderm.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Ctenophores are diploblastic (ectoderm, endoderm and mesoglea). R is false because they lack mesoderm.
steps: A: ctenophores are diploblastic. True.
R: they have a well-formed mesoderm. False: they have mesoglea, not mesoderm.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks the middle layer of ctenophores is mesoderm

teach.ask: Gappu tries to fold a starfish and an earthworm into equal halves. Explain symmetry and germ layers to him!
teach.praise: Chirp! Radial for starfish, bilateral for worms, and two or three germ layers. Super!
teach.nudge: Nice! What is the difference between diploblastic and triploblastic?

revise.summary: Animals may be asymmetrical (most sponges), radially symmetrical (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms) or bilaterally symmetrical. Diploblastic animals have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea; triploblastic animals add mesoderm.
focus: Asymmetry, radial and bilateral symmetry with examples
Diploblastic vs triploblastic organisation
Mesoglea vs mesoderm
remember: Radial: any plane through central axis gives identical halves
Bilateral: only one plane gives identical left and right halves
Diploblastic: coelenterates, ctenophores; triploblastic: Platyhelminthes to chordates
traps: Don't call mesoglea a germ layer
Don't forget echinoderm larvae are bilateral though adults are radial

learn.hook: A body cavity is like a padded room inside you where organs can move and grow. Not every animal has one, and some have a 'fake' one.
points: Coelom: a body cavity lined by mesoderm. Coelomates: annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates.
Pseudocoelom: the cavity is not lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm (Aschelminthes). Acoelomates have no body cavity (Platyhelminthes).
Metameric segmentation (metamerism): the body is divided externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of some organs, as in the earthworm.

Notochord: a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development. Animals with it are chordates; those without are non-chordates (Porifera to Echinodermata).

Broad flowchart: cellular level (Porifera) → tissue level, diploblastic, radial (Coelenterata, Ctenophora) → triploblastic acoelomate (Platyhelminthes), pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes), coelomate (annelids onwards) → notochord (Chordata).

example.q: An animal is triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, with a body cavity not lined by mesoderm. Name its phylum.
steps: Triploblastic and bilateral rules out sponges and coelenterates.
A cavity with scattered mesoderm pouches is a pseudocoelom.
Pseudocoelomates are Aschelminthes.

learn.reallife: Farmers in Punjab value earthworms as 'friends of farmers'; their segmented body is a textbook example of metamerism.

quiz.q: A body cavity lined by mesoderm is called a:
quiz.explain: A true coelom is lined by mesoderm.
steps: A true coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm.
A pseudocoelom is not lined by mesoderm.
Answer: Coelom

quiz.q: Aschelminthes are:
quiz.explain: Their mesoderm is in scattered pouches, giving a pseudocoelom.
steps: In Aschelminthes mesoderm is in scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm.
The cavity is not lined by mesoderm, so it is a pseudocoelom.
Answer: Pseudocoelomates

quiz.q: Which phylum is acoelomate?
quiz.explain: Flatworms have no body cavity.
steps: Acoelomates have no body cavity.
Platyhelminthes (flatworms) are acoelomate.
Annelids, chordates and molluscs are coelomates.
Answer: Platyhelminthes

quiz.q: Metameric segmentation is best seen in:
quiz.explain: Earthworm segments show serial repetition of organs.
steps: Metamerism: body divided externally and internally into segments with organs repeated.
This is best seen in the earthworm.
Answer: Earthworm

quiz.q: The notochord is derived from which germ layer?
quiz.explain: The notochord is mesodermally derived.
steps: The notochord is a rod formed during embryonic development.
It is mesodermally derived.
Answer: Mesoderm
quiz.mistake: Thinks it comes from ectoderm like the nerve cord

quiz.q: The notochord forms on which side of the embryo?
quiz.explain: It forms on the dorsal side during embryonic development.
steps: The notochord forms on the dorsal side of the embryo.
Answer: Dorsal side

quiz.q: Which group of phyla are all non-chordates?
quiz.explain: Animals from Porifera to Echinodermata lack a notochord.
steps: Animals without a notochord are non-chordates.
These are Porifera to Echinodermata.
Answer: Porifera to Echinodermata

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ascaris has a pseudocoelom. Reason (R): In Ascaris, mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between the ectoderm and the endoderm.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; scattered mesoderm pouches (instead of a lining) is what makes the cavity a pseudocoelom.
steps: A: Ascaris has a pseudocoelom. True.
R: mesoderm is in scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm. True.
That arrangement defines a pseudocoelom, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why the cavity is called false

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why some worms are 'acoelomate' and others 'coelomate'. Explain body cavities, segmentation and the notochord!
teach.praise: Tweet! True, false or no cavity, plus segments and a notochord. Classification unlocked!
teach.nudge: Good! What lines a true coelom, and which animals have a notochord?

revise.summary: A coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm; a pseudocoelom has scattered mesoderm pouches (Aschelminthes); acoelomates (flatworms) have none. Earthworms show metameric segmentation, and a dorsal mesodermal notochord marks chordates.

Metameric segmentation

remember: Coelom: lined by mesoderm
Pseudocoelomate: Aschelminthes; acoelomate: Platyhelminthes
Notochord: mesodermal, dorsal, formed in embryo
Non-chordates: Porifera to Echinodermata
traps: Don't call Aschelminthes acoelomate; they are pseudocoelomate
Don't say the notochord is ectodermal or ventral

learn.hook: Swimmers in the Andaman Sea learn to respect jellyfish tentacles. Each one is loaded with thousands of tiny harpoons.
points: Porifera (sponges): mostly marine, asymmetrical, cellular level. A water canal system: water enters through ostia into the spongocoel and leaves by the osculum; it helps in food gathering, gas exchange and waste removal. Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and canals. Digestion is intracellular. Skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres. Hermaphrodite; asexual reproduction by fragmentation; fertilisation internal; development indirect. Sycon, Spongilla (freshwater), Euspongia (bath sponge).

Coelenterata (Cnidaria): aquatic, mostly marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) with nematocysts on tentacles are used for anchorage, defence and prey capture. Gastrovascular cavity with a single opening, the mouth on the hypostome; digestion extracellular and intracellular. Corals have a calcium carbonate skeleton.

Two body forms: polyp (sessile, cylindrical; Hydra, Adamsia) and medusa (umbrella-shaped, free-swimming; Aurelia). In Obelia, polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually: metagenesis (alternation of generation). Examples: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (sea anemone), Pennatula (sea-pen), Gorgonia (sea-fan), Meandrina (brain coral).

Ctenophora (sea walnuts or comb jellies): exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates help locomotion. Bioluminescence is well marked. Sexes not separate; only sexual reproduction; external fertilisation; indirect development. Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana.

example.q: Trace the path of water through a sponge.
steps: Water enters through tiny pores, the ostia.
It passes into the central cavity, the spongocoel, lined by choanocytes.
It exits through the osculum.

learn.reallife: Coral reefs of the Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep and the Andamans are built by coelenterates and are protected marine areas in India.

quiz.q: Water leaves a sponge through the:
quiz.explain: Water enters by ostia and exits through the osculum.
steps: Sponge water path: ostia → spongocoel → osculum.
Water leaves through the osculum.
Ostia are where water enters.
Answer: Osculum

quiz.q: Collar cells lining the spongocoel are called:
quiz.explain: Choanocytes line the spongocoel and canals.
steps: The spongocoel and canals are lined by collar cells.
These are choanocytes.
Cnidoblasts are stinging cells of coelenterates.
Answer: Choanocytes
quiz.mistake: Confuses sponge cells with cnidarian cells

quiz.q: Cnidoblasts are used for:
quiz.explain: Stinging cnidoblasts with nematocysts help hold, defend and capture.
steps: Cnidoblasts carry nematocysts on the tentacles.
They are used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey.
Answer: Anchorage, defence and capture of prey
options: Anchorage, defence and capture of prey

quiz.q: Alternation between polyp and medusa forms is called:
quiz.explain: In Obelia, polyps make medusae asexually and medusae make polyps sexually.
steps: In Obelia, polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually.
This alternation is called metagenesis.
Metamerism is segmentation, not this.
Answer: Metagenesis

quiz.q: Comb plates of ctenophores help in:
quiz.explain: The eight rows of ciliated comb plates help the animal swim.
steps: Ctenophores have eight external rows of ciliated comb plates.
These help in locomotion.
Answer: Locomotion
quiz.mistake: Thinks comb plates sting like cnidoblasts

quiz.q: Which is a freshwater sponge?
quiz.explain: Spongilla lives in fresh water.
steps: Spongilla is the freshwater sponge.
Sycon and Euspongia are marine; Physalia is a coelenterate.
Answer: Spongilla

quiz.q: Digestion in coelenterates is:
quiz.explain: Food is partly digested in the gastrovascular cavity and finished inside cells.
steps: Coelenterates partly digest food in the gastrovascular cavity (extracellular).
Digestion is completed inside cells (intracellular).
Answer: Both extracellular and intracellular

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Sponges have separate male and female individuals. Reason (R): In sponges, eggs and sperms are produced by the same individual.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: sponges are hermaphrodites, not dioecious. R is true: one sponge produces both eggs and sperms, which is what hermaphrodite means.
steps: A: sponges have separate male and female individuals. False: they are hermaphrodite.
R: one sponge produces both eggs and sperms. True.
So A is false, R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu got stung by a jellyfish at the beach. Explain cnidoblasts and how sponges and comb jellies are different!
teach.praise: Chirp! Stinging cells for jellyfish, water canals for sponges, comb plates for ctenophores. Ouch, but cool!
teach.nudge: Good! What stung me, and what makes sponges and comb jellies special?

revise.summary: Sponges are cellular-level animals with a water canal system (ostia → spongocoel → osculum) and choanocytes. Coelenterates are diploblastic with cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa forms and metagenesis. Ctenophores move by eight rows of comb plates.

Cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa, metagenesis
Comb plates and bioluminescence in ctenophores
Examples of each phylum
remember: Porifera: Sycon, Spongilla (freshwater), Euspongia; hermaphrodite, intracellular digestion
Coelenterata: Hydra, Adamsia, Aurelia, Obelia, Physalia, Meandrina
Ctenophora: Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana; 8 rows of comb plates
traps: Don't swap ostia (water in) and osculum (water out)
Don't confuse metagenesis with metamerism

learn.hook: Deworming tablets are given to crores of Indian children on National Deworming Day. The targets are flatworms and roundworms.
points: Platyhelminthes (flatworms): dorsoventrally flattened, mostly endoparasites; bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level. Hooks and suckers in parasites; some absorb nutrients through the body surface. Flame cells help osmoregulation and excretion. Sexes not separate; fertilisation internal; many larval stages. Planaria has high regeneration capacity. Taenia (tapeworm), Fasciola (liver fluke).

Aschelminthes (roundworms): circular in cross-section; free-living or parasitic; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate. Complete alimentary canal with a muscular pharynx; an excretory tube opens by an excretory pore. Dioecious, with females often longer than males (sexual dimorphism). Fertilisation internal; development direct or indirect. Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filarial worm), Ancylostoma (hookworm).

Annelida: aquatic or terrestrial; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, metamerically segmented. Longitudinal and circular muscles help locomotion; Nereis has parapodia for swimming.

Annelids have a closed circulatory system and nephridia for osmoregulation and excretion; the nervous system has paired ganglia joined to a double ventral nerve cord. Nereis is dioecious; earthworms and leeches are monoecious. Pheretima (earthworm), Hirudinaria (blood-sucking leech).

example.q: A worm is circular in cross-section, has separate sexes with a longer female and a complete gut. Name its phylum and one example.
steps: Circular cross-section suggests roundworm.
Separate sexes with sexual dimorphism and a complete gut fit Aschelminthes.

learn.reallife: Wuchereria causes lymphatic filariasis, which India aims to eliminate through mass drug administration campaigns.

quiz.q: Flame cells in flatworms help in:
quiz.explain: Flame cells remove wastes and regulate water.
steps: Flame cells are found in flatworms.
They help in osmoregulation and excretion.
Answer: Osmoregulation and excretion

quiz.q: Which flatworm shows high regeneration capacity?
quiz.explain: Planaria can regrow lost parts.
steps: Planaria is a flatworm with high regeneration capacity.
Taenia and Fasciola are parasites; Ascaris is a roundworm.
Answer: Planaria

quiz.q: Wuchereria is commonly known as the:
quiz.explain: Wuchereria causes filariasis.
steps: Wuchereria is a roundworm that causes filariasis.
So it is the filarial worm.
Ancylostoma is the hookworm.
Answer: Filarial worm

quiz.q: Lateral appendages that help Nereis swim are called:
quiz.explain: Parapodia are paddle-like appendages of Nereis.
steps: Nereis is an annelid that swims.
Its lateral paddle-like appendages are parapodia.
Pseudopodia belong to amoeboid protists.
Answer: Parapodia

quiz.q: Excretion and osmoregulation in annelids are carried out by:
quiz.explain: Annelids use nephridia.
steps: Annelids osmoregulate and excrete with nephridia.
Malpighian tubules are insect organs; flame cells are flatworm organs.
Answer: Nephridia
quiz.mistake: Gives the flatworm or insect organ

quiz.q: Which annelid is dioecious?
quiz.explain: Nereis has separate sexes; earthworms and leeches are monoecious.
steps: Nereis has separate sexes (dioecious).
Earthworms (Pheretima) and leeches are monoecious.
Answer: Nereis

quiz.q: Roundworms show sexual dimorphism, meaning:
quiz.explain: Separate sexes that look different is sexual dimorphism.
steps: Roundworms are dioecious.
Males and females look different; females are often longer.
That difference is sexual dimorphism.
Answer: Males and females look different, females often longer
options: Males and females look different, females often longer

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Annelids have a closed circulatory system. Reason (R): Annelids are acoelomate.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Annelids do have closed circulation (A true), but they are true coelomates, so R is false.
steps: A: annelids have closed circulation. True.
R: annelids are acoelomate. False: they are coelomate.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false

teach.ask: Gappu's school is giving deworming tablets. Explain the three worm phyla so he knows his enemies (and his friend the earthworm)!
teach.praise: Tweet! Flat, round and segmented. And the earthworm is the friendly one!
teach.nudge: Good! What body cavity does each worm group have?

revise.summary: Flatworms are flattened, acoelomate, mostly parasitic, with flame cells. Roundworms are pseudocoelomate, dioecious with a complete gut. Annelids are segmented coelomates with closed circulation, nephridia and a double ventral nerve cord.

learn.hook: More than two out of every three named species on Earth are arthropods. Honeybees, silkworms, mosquitoes and crabs all wear armour.
points: Arthropoda: the largest phylum (over two-thirds of named species). Organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, segmented, coelomate. Chitinous exoskeleton; body of head, thorax and abdomen; jointed appendages (arthros = joint, poda = appendages).

Arthropods breathe by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae; circulation is open; excretion by Malpighian tubules; senses include antennae, compound and simple eyes and statocysts. Mostly dioecious, fertilisation usually internal, mostly oviparous.

Arthropod examples: Apis (honeybee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect) are useful; Anopheles, Culex and Aedes (mosquitoes) are vectors; Locusta (locust) is a gregarious pest; Limulus (king crab) is a living fossil.

Mollusca: the second largest phylum; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate. Unsegmented soft body with a calcareous shell, distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump. The mantle covers the hump; feather-like gills in the mantle cavity do respiration and excretion. Head has sensory tentacles; the mouth has a rasping, file-like radula.

Molluscs are usually dioecious and oviparous with indirect development. Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia (cuttlefish), Loligo (squid), Octopus (devil fish), Aplysia (sea-hare), Dentalium (tusk shell), Chaetopleura (chiton).

learn.hook: A starfish walks on hundreds of tiny water-filled feet and has no excretory system at all. Strange, but true.
points: Echinodermata (spiny-skinned): endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles; all marine; organ-system level; triploblastic, coelomate. Adults are radially symmetrical, larvae bilaterally symmetrical.

Complete gut with mouth on the lower (ventral) side and anus on the upper (dorsal) side. The water vascular system, their most distinctive feature, helps locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration. There is no excretory system. Sexes separate; fertilisation usually external; development indirect with a free-swimming larva.
Examples: Asterias (starfish), Echinus (sea urchin), Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Ophiura (brittle star).

Hemichordata: small group of worm-like marine animals, once a sub-phylum of Chordata, now a separate non-chordate phylum. Body of proboscis, collar and trunk. A rudimentary stomochord in the collar is similar to a notochord. Open circulation; respiration by gills; excretion by a proboscis gland; sexes separate; external fertilisation; indirect development. Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus.

Signature features to remember: water canal system (Porifera), cnidoblasts (Coelenterata), comb plates (Ctenophora), flame cells (Platyhelminthes), parapodia (Nereis), Malpighian tubules (insects), radula (Mollusca), water vascular system (Echinodermata).

example.q: Why are Balanoglossus and its relatives no longer placed in Chordata?
steps: They have only a stomochord in the collar, a rudimentary structure similar to a notochord, not a true notochord.
So they are placed in a separate phylum, Hemichordata, under non-chordates.
example.answer: They lack a true notochord; the stomochord is only notochord-like.

topics.title: Phylum Chordata: key features and subphyla

learn.hook: A tiny sea squirt larva has a notochord in its tail, then loses it as an adult. Yet both it and you are chordates.
points: Fundamental chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail. Chordates are bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, at organ-system level, with a closed circulatory system.

Chordates vs non-chordates: notochord present vs absent; nerve cord dorsal, hollow, single vs ventral, solid, double; pharynx with gill slits vs no gill slits; heart ventral vs dorsal (if present); post-anal tail present vs absent.

Subphyla: Urochordata (Tunicata), notochord only in the larval tail (Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum); Cephalochordata, notochord from head to tail throughout life (Branchiostoma, also called Amphioxus or lancelet); Vertebrata.

Vertebrates have a notochord only in the embryo; it is replaced by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column. They have a ventral muscular heart (2, 3 or 4 chambers), kidneys and paired appendages (fins or limbs). All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates.

Vertebrata: Agnatha (no jaws; class Cyclostomata) and Gnathostomata (jaws; superclass Pisces with fins: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes; superclass Tetrapoda with limbs: Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia).

learn.reallife: The soft jelly-like core of each disc in your spine is a remnant of your embryonic notochord, which is why spine surgeons treating slipped discs care about it.

learn.hook: Sharks must keep swimming or they sink, while a rohu in a Bengal pond can hover still. The secret is an air bladder.
points: Cyclostomata: jawless ectoparasites on fishes; elongated body with 6–15 pairs of gill slits; sucking circular mouth without jaws; no scales or paired fins; cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column; closed circulation. Marine, but migrate to fresh water to spawn, and die within a few days; larvae return to the ocean. Petromyzon (lamprey), Myxine (hagfish).

Chondrichthyes: marine, streamlined, cartilaginous endoskeleton; ventral mouth; notochord persists throughout life; gill slits separate, no operculum; tough skin with minute placoid scales; teeth are modified placoid scales directed backwards. No air bladder, so they swim constantly to avoid sinking. Two-chambered heart; cold-blooded.

Chondrichthyes contd.: some have electric organs (Torpedo) or a poison sting (Trygon); males have claspers on pelvic fins; internal fertilisation; many viviparous. Scoliodon (dogfish), Pristis (sawfish), Carcharodon (great white shark), Trygon (stingray).

Osteichthyes: marine and freshwater, bony endoskeleton; mouth mostly terminal; four pairs of gills covered by an operculum on each side; cycloid or ctenoid scales; air bladder regulates buoyancy; two-chambered heart; cold-blooded; fertilisation usually external; mostly oviparous, development direct.
Osteichthyes examples: Exocoetus (flying fish), Hippocampus (sea horse), Labeo (rohu), Catla (katla), Clarias (magur), Betta (fighting fish), Pterophyllum (angel fish).

learn.hook: A frog breathes through its skin, and a crocodile has a four-chambered heart like ours. Tetrapods start getting interesting.
points: Amphibia: live in water and on land; most have two pairs of limbs; body of head and trunk; moist skin without scales; eyelids; a tympanum represents the ear.

Amphibians: the gut, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common cloaca; respiration by gills, lungs and skin; three-chambered heart (two auricles, one ventricle); cold-blooded; sexes separate; external fertilisation; oviparous; development indirect. Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra (salamander), Ichthyophis (limbless amphibian).
Reptilia (Latin repere, to creep): mostly terrestrial; dry, cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes; no external ear openings, a tympanum represents the ear; limbs, when present, two pairs.

Reptiles: heart usually three-chambered but four-chambered in crocodiles; poikilotherms; snakes and lizards shed scales as skin cast; internal fertilisation; oviparous; development direct. Chelone (turtle), Testudo (tortoise), Chameleon (tree lizard), Calotes (garden lizard), Crocodilus (crocodile), Alligator, Hemidactylus (wall lizard), and poisonous snakes Naja (cobra), Bangarus (krait), Vipera (viper).

example.answer: Frog: external fertilisation, indirect development. Lizard: internal fertilisation, direct development.

quiz.explain: Shedding skin cast is true, but reptiles are poikilotherms (cold-blooded), so R is false.
steps: A: snakes and lizards shed scales as skin cast. True.
R: reptiles are warm-blooded. False: they are poikilotherms.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Confuses reptiles with birds and mammals

teach.ask: Gappu finds a frog and a garden lizard in the garden. Explain how amphibians and reptiles differ!
teach.praise: Chirp! Moist skin and outside fertilisation for frogs, dry scales and inside fertilisation for lizards!
teach.nudge: Good! How is their skin different, and where does fertilisation happen?

revise.summary: Amphibians live on land and in water, have moist scaleless skin, a cloaca, a three-chambered heart, external fertilisation and indirect development. Reptiles have dry cornified skin with scales, are cold-blooded, fertilise internally and develop directly.
focus: Amphibian features: skin, cloaca, heart, respiration, development
Reptile features: skin, heart (crocodile exception), skin cast, development
Examples of amphibians and reptiles, including poisonous snakes
remember: Amphibian heart: 2 auricles + 1 ventricle
Crocodile: four-chambered heart
Amphibians: Bufo, Rana, Hyla, Salamandra, Ichthyophis (limbless)
Poisonous snakes: Naja, Bangarus, Vipera
traps: Don't call reptiles warm-blooded
Don't call Ichthyophis a snake; it is a limbless amphibian

learn.hook: A peacock's bones are hollow like bamboo, and a platypus lays eggs yet feeds its young milk. Nature loves exceptions.
points: Aves: feathers; most fly (flightless: ostrich); beak; forelimbs modified into wings; hind limbs scaly, adapted for walking, swimming or perching. Dry skin with only an oil gland at the base of the tail.

Birds: fully ossified endoskeleton with hollow, air-filled (pneumatic) long bones; crop and gizzard in the gut; completely four-chambered heart; warm-blooded (homoiothermous); lungs with air sacs; internal fertilisation; oviparous; direct development. Corvus (crow), Columba (pigeon), Psittacula (parrot), Struthio (ostrich), Pavo (peacock), Aptenodytes (penguin), Neophron (vulture).

Mammalia: mammary glands (milk-producing) are the most unique feature. Two pairs of limbs adapted for walking, running, climbing, burrowing, swimming or flying. Hair on the skin; external ears (pinnae); different types of teeth; four-chambered heart; homoiothermous; lungs.

Mammals: sexes separate, internal fertilisation; viviparous with few exceptions; development direct. Oviparous: Ornithorhynchus (platypus). Viviparous: Macropus (kangaroo), Pteropus (flying fox), Camelus, Macaca (monkey), Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Equus, Delphinus (dolphin), Balaenoptera (blue whale), Panthera tigris, Panthera leo.

example.q: A dolphin lives in water and has flippers. Give two features that show it is a mammal, not a fish.
steps: It has mammary glands and feeds its young on milk.
It breathes with lungs and is warm-blooded, with a four-chambered heart.
example.answer: Mammary glands and lung breathing (also warm-blooded, viviparous).

learn.reallife: The Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus) is India's national bird, the Bengal tiger the national animal, and the Ganges river dolphin the national aquatic animal.

quiz.q: Pneumatic bones are found in:
quiz.explain: Birds have hollow long bones with air cavities.
steps: Pneumatic bones are hollow long bones with air cavities.
They are found in birds.
Answer: Birds

quiz.q: The most unique feature of mammals is:
quiz.explain: Birds also have four chambers and lungs; mammary glands are found only in mammals.
steps: Birds also have lungs, internal fertilisation and a four-chambered heart.
Only mammals have mammary glands.
So mammary glands are the most unique feature.
Answer: Mammary glands
quiz.mistake: Picks a feature shared with birds

quiz.q: Which mammal lays eggs?
quiz.explain: The platypus is an oviparous mammal.
steps: Mammals are viviparous with few exceptions.
Ornithorhynchus (platypus) is oviparous.
Answer: Ornithorhynchus

quiz.q: The skin of birds has only one gland, the:
quiz.explain: Bird skin is dry with only an oil gland near the tail.
steps: Bird skin is dry.
Its only gland is the oil gland at the base of the tail.
Answer: Oil gland at the base of the tail
options: Oil gland at the base of the tail

quiz.q: Additional chambers in the bird digestive tract are:
quiz.explain: The crop stores food and the gizzard grinds it.
steps: Birds have extra chambers in the gut.
The crop stores food and the gizzard grinds it.
Answer: Crop and gizzard

quiz.q: Which bird is flightless?
quiz.explain: Struthio (ostrich) cannot fly.
steps: Most birds fly.
Struthio (ostrich) is flightless.
Answer: Struthio

quiz.q: Pteropus is a:
quiz.explain: Pteropus is a bat, a mammal adapted for flight.
steps: Pteropus is the flying fox, a bat.
It is a flying mammal.
Answer: Flying mammal (flying fox)
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything that flies is a bird

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Birds and mammals can live in very cold and very hot places. Reason (R): Birds and mammals are homoiothermous and keep a constant body temperature.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; a constant body temperature lets them stay active in extreme climates.
steps: A: birds and mammals live in very cold and very hot places. True.
R: they are homoiothermous, keeping a constant body temperature. True.
Constant temperature lets them survive extremes, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link warm-bloodedness to habitat range

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'A penguin swims and a bat flies. Which is the bird?' Explain the features of birds and mammals!
teach.praise: Tweet! Feathers and hollow bones for birds, milk and hair for mammals. Penguin is a bird, bat is a mammal!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the one feature only mammals have? And what about birds?

revise.summary: Birds have feathers, wings, beaks, pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard, a four-chambered heart and are warm-blooded and oviparous. Mammals have mammary glands, hair, pinnae, different teeth and a four-chambered heart, and are mostly viviparous.
focus: Bird features and adaptations for flight
Mammal features, especially mammary glands
Exceptions: flightless ostrich, egg-laying platypus
Examples of birds and mammals
remember: Birds: pneumatic bones, oil gland only, crop and gizzard, air sacs
Mammals' most unique feature: mammary glands
Ornithorhynchus: oviparous mammal; Pteropus: flying fox
traps: Don't say a four-chambered heart is unique to mammals; birds have it too
Don't call all mammals viviparous; the platypus lays eggs

topics.title: Salient features of the phyla: putting it together

learn.hook: Board exams love a 'which phylum is this?' question. Master the summary table and you can crack any of them.
points: Porifera: cellular level, asymmetrical, canal system. Coelenterata and Ctenophora: tissue level, radial, diploblastic.
Platyhelminthes: organ level, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, incomplete gut. Aschelminthes: pseudocoelomate, complete gut. Annelida: coelomate, segmented, closed circulation.

Arthropoda: segmented, jointed appendages, open circulation. Mollusca: unsegmented, open circulation. Echinodermata: adult radial, coelomate, water vascular system, complete gut. Hemichordata: open circulation. Chordata: notochord, closed circulation.
Direct development: young resemble adults (e.g. reptiles, birds, mammals, bony fish). Indirect development: a larval stage different from the adult (e.g. sponges, echinoderms, amphibians).
Open circulation in arthropods, molluscs and hemichordates; closed in annelids and chordates.

example.q: Identify the phylum: triploblastic, coelomate, segmented, jointed appendages, open circulation.
steps: Segmented coelomates: annelids or arthropods.
Jointed appendages and open circulation point to arthropods.

learn.reallife: A visit to the Zoological Survey of India's museum in Kolkata shows specimens arranged phylum by phylum, much like this summary table.

quiz.q: An animal is bilateral, triploblastic, has no body cavity and a gut with one opening. It belongs to:
quiz.explain: Acoelomate with an incomplete gut fits flatworms.
steps: Bilateral, triploblastic, no body cavity = acoelomate.
A gut with one opening = incomplete.
These fit Platyhelminthes.
Answer: Platyhelminthes

quiz.q: Which pair both have open circulation?
quiz.explain: Arthropods and molluscs have open circulation; annelids and chordates have closed.
steps: Open circulation: arthropods, molluscs, hemichordates.
Closed circulation: annelids and chordates.
So the pair is Arthropoda and Mollusca.
Answer: Arthropoda and Mollusca
quiz.mistake: Pairs one open with one closed

quiz.q: Which phylum has radial symmetry in adults and is coelomate?
quiz.explain: Coelenterates and ctenophores are radial but not coelomate.
steps: Coelenterata and Ctenophora are radial but not coelomate.
Echinoderm adults are radial and they are coelomate.
Answer: Echinodermata

quiz.q: Indirect development means:
quiz.explain: A distinct larva shows indirect development.
steps: Indirect development has a larval stage.
The larva differs from the adult.
Answer: There is a larval stage that differs from the adult
options: There is a larval stage that differs from the adult
The young look exactly like the adult
The embryo grows in the mother

quiz.q: Which phylum is segmented and coelomate but has closed circulation?
quiz.explain: Annelids are segmented coelomates with closed circulation.
steps: Segmented coelomates are annelids and arthropods.
Arthropods have open circulation; annelids closed.
Answer: Annelida

quiz.q: A marine animal is diploblastic with eight rows of comb plates. Its phylum is:
quiz.explain: Comb plates are diagnostic of ctenophores.
steps: Diploblastic and marine narrows it to coelenterates or ctenophores.
Eight rows of comb plates are diagnostic of ctenophores.
Answer: Ctenophora

quiz.q: Which group shows direct development?
quiz.explain: Birds hatch as miniature adults; the others have larvae.
steps: Direct development: young resemble adults (reptiles, birds, mammals).
Starfish, sponges and frogs have larvae.
Answer: Birds

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Molluscs and arthropods both have open circulation. Reason (R): Molluscs and arthropods are both segmented.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both do have open circulation, but molluscs are unsegmented, so R is false.
steps: A: molluscs and arthropods have open circulation. True.
R: both are segmented. False: molluscs are unsegmented.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks molluscs are segmented like arthropods

teach.ask: Gappu has a pile of clue cards: 'jointed legs', 'flame cells', 'tube feet'. Show him how to use the summary table to find the phylum!
teach.praise: Chirp! Symmetry, coelom, circulation and development: the four keys to every phylum!
teach.nudge: Good! Which features would you check first to place an animal in a phylum?

revise.summary: Each phylum has a signature set of features: level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, gut, circulation and development. Combining these lets you identify any phylum from a description.
focus: Identifying a phylum from a set of features
Which phyla have open vs closed circulation
Direct vs indirect development with examples
remember: Open circulation: Arthropoda, Mollusca, Hemichordata; closed: Annelida, Chordata
Acoelomate: Platyhelminthes; pseudocoelomate: Aschelminthes
Direct development: reptiles, birds, mammals; indirect: sponges, echinoderms, amphibians
traps: Don't call molluscs segmented
Don't call coelenterates or ctenophores coelomate just because they are radial
